claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claims.claim: CMV is a highly prevalent pathogen that usually induces high T cell frequencies.
claims.source: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a highly prevalent pathogen and usually induces high T cell frequencies, making CMV a potential trigger for cross-reactive SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells (Sylwester et al., 2005; Zuhair et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sylwester et al., 2005 and Zuhair et al., 2019.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were increased in CMV-seropositive donors.
claims.source: This is supported by the finding that SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were increased in CMV-seropositive (CMV+) donors and that previous CMV infection has been associated with severe COVID-19 (Alanio et al., 2022; Jo et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Previous CMV infection has been associated with severe COVID-19.
claims.source: This is supported by the finding that SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were increased in CMV-seropositive (CMV+) donors and that previous CMV infection has been associated with severe COVID-19 (Alanio et al., 2022; Jo et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: All CMV+ donors displayed a CD4+ and/or CD8+ T cell response upon stimulation with pp65.
claims.source: As expected, all CMV+ donors displayed a CD4+ and/or CD8+ T cell response upon stimulation with pp65 (Figure 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claims.claim: Six donors in the CMV+ group displayed a CD4+ T cell response against the membrane peptide pool which was not observed in the CMV− group.
claims.source: However, six donors in the CMV+ group displayed a CD4+ T cell response against the membrane peptide pool which was not observed in the CMV− group (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: CD4+ T cell response against the membrane pool was accompanied by a CD4+ T cell response against pp65.
claims.source: Furthermore, CD4+ T cell response against the membrane pool was accompanied by a CD4+ T cell response against pp65 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: CD8+ T cell responses were detected against spike peptides in two CMV+ donors which were not detected in CMV− donors.
claims.source: In addition, CD8+ T cell responses were detected against spike peptides in two CMV+ donors which were not detected in CMV− donors (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Donors with a high CD8+ T cell response against SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides additionally displayed strong reactivity against pp65.
claims.source: Interestingly, donors with a high CD8+ T cell response against SARS-CoV-2 spike peptides additionally displayed strong reactivity against pp65 (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: 20 out of 27 screened T cell clones produced IFN-γ when stimulated with membrane peptide pool.
claims.source: After clonal expansion, 20 out of 27 screened T cell clones produced IFN-γ when stimulated with membrane peptide pool compared to no peptide stimulation (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated as experimental data, though the data is not shown.

claims.claim: T cell clones 4UGT5, 4UGT8, and 4UGT17 all express different TCRs.
claims.source: T cell clones 4UGT5, 4UGT8, and 4UGT17, all three expressing a different TCR, were used for further experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The CD4+ T cell clones were reactive against both SARS-CoV-2 membrane antigen and CMV pp65 when loaded on HLA-matched EBV-LCLs.
claims.source: As hypothesized, the T cell clones were reactive against both SARS-CoV-2 membrane antigen and CMV pp65 when loaded on HLA-matched EBV-lymphoblastoid cell lines (EBV-LCLs; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: IFN-γ production by the CD4+ T cell clones was significantly increased when stimulated with pp65 peptides compared to membrane peptides.
claims.source: Interestingly, IFN-γ production by the T cell clones was significantly increased when stimulated with pp65 peptides compared to membrane peptides, indicating higher avidity for CMV compared to SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: T cell clone 4UGT8 recognizes pp65 peptide AGILARNLVPM.
claims.source: To identify which peptide in pp65 is recognized, reactivity of T cell clone 4UGT8 against a pp65 library was measured which resulted in recognition of three sub pools which contained peptide AGILARNLVPM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C.

claims.claim: T cell clone 4UGT8 recognized both peptide pools and the AGI peptide only when presented in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
claims.source: T cell clone 4UGT8 recognized both peptide pools and the AGI peptide only when presented in HLA-DRB3*02:02 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: 23 out of 28 CD8+ T cell clones produced IFN-γ upon spike peptide pool stimulation.
claims.source: The isolated CD8+ T cell clones were screened for their reactivity with SARS-CoV-2 spike which showed that 23 out of the 28 T cell clones produced IFN-γ upon spike peptide pool stimulation (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated as experimental data, though the data is not shown.

claims.claim: All 23 spike-reactive CD8+ T cell clones expressed the same TCR.
claims.source: TCR sequencing revealed that all 23T cell clones expressed the same TCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: T cell clone 8UTT6 recognized spike as well as pp65 peptide pool presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-B*35:01.
claims.source: The results confirmed that T cell clone 8UTT6 recognized spike as well as pp65 peptide pool presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-B*35:01 but not transduced with HLA-A*11:01 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: T cell clone 8UTT6 did not recognize spike or pp65 peptide pools when presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-A*11:01.
claims.source: The results confirmed that T cell clone 8UTT6 recognized spike as well as pp65 peptide pool presented by K562 cells transduced with HLA-B*35:01 but not transduced with HLA-A*11:01 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The FVS and IPS peptides were recognized by clone 8UTT6.
claims.source: The FVS and IPS peptides were indeed recognized by clone 8UTT6 (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The IPS peptide was recognized with higher avidity compared to the FVS peptide by clone 8UTT6.
claims.source: Importantly, the IPS peptide was recognized with higher avidity compared to the FVS peptide by clone 8UTT6 (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by peptide titration data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The same TCRβ chain was already described and demonstrated to be specific for IPS in HLA-B*35:01.
claims.source: Supporting these findings, the same TCRβ chain was already described and demonstrated to be specific for IPS in HLA-B*35:01 (Klarenbeek et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Klarenbeek et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The two peptides IPS and FVS share two residues (P3-S and P7-H).
claims.source: The two peptides share two residues (P3-S and P7-H) and have two similar residues (P6-T/V and P9-F/Y) based on similar biochemical properties and size.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis described in the text.

claims.claim: The two peptides IPS and FVS have two similar residues (P6-T/V and P9-F/Y) based on similar biochemical properties and size.
claims.source: The two peptides share two residues (P3-S and P7-H) and have two similar residues (P6-T/V and P9-F/Y) based on similar biochemical properties and size.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis described in the text.

claims.claim: Not all T cells that bound to B*35/IPS-tetramer were able to bind to the B*35/FVS-tetramer.
claims.source: Tetramer staining of PBMCs from donor UTT demonstrated that not all T cells that bound to B*35/IPS-tetramer were able to bind to the B*35/FVS-tetramer as well.
claims.evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: All T cells that bound to B*35/FVS-tetramer were also binding to the B*35/IPS-tetramer.
claims.source: However, all T cells that bound to B*35/FVS-tetramer were also binding to the B*35/IPS-tetramer (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS cross-reactivity is dictated by specific TCR sequences.
claims.source: This observation indicates that IPS/FVS cross-reactivity is dictated by specific TCR sequences which were further supported by the lack of binding to B*35/FVS-tetramer by an IPS-specific T cell clone with a different TCR (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Nearly all CMV+ donors had IPS-specific T cells with frequencies above background level.
claims.source: Screening of SARS-CoV-2-unexposed, CMV+, and HLA-B*35(:01) donors (N=37) showed that nearly all CMV+ donors had IPS-specific T cells with frequencies above background level, and interestingly, three of the analyzed donors (UTT, UBV, and SFW) presented with clearly detectable IPS/FVS-specific T cells (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Three donors (UTT, UBV, and SFW) presented with clearly detectable IPS/FVS-specific T cells.
claims.source: Screening of SARS-CoV-2-unexposed, CMV+, and HLA-B*35(:01) donors (N=37) showed that nearly all CMV+ donors had IPS-specific T cells with frequencies above background level, and interestingly, three of the analyzed donors (UTT, UBV, and SFW) presented with clearly detectable IPS/FVS-specific T cells (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells displayed an effector memory phenotype (CCR7−CD45RA−).
claims.source: Furthermore, IPS/FVS-specific T cells displayed an effector memory phenotype (CCR7−CD45RA−), confirming a memory repertoire origin and, interestingly, a less differentiated phenotype compared to IPS-specific T cells (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells have a less differentiated phenotype compared to IPS-specific T cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, IPS/FVS-specific T cells displayed an effector memory phenotype (CCR7−CD45RA−), confirming a memory repertoire origin and, interestingly, a less differentiated phenotype compared to IPS-specific T cells (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant CDR3 of the α-chain, CAGNQGGKLIF.
claims.source: Interestingly, B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant complementary-determining region 3 (CDR3) of the α-chain, CAGNQGGKLIF (CDR3αCAGNQG), and β-chain, CASSLALDEQFF (CDR3βCASSLA; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant CDR3 of the β-chain, CASSLALDEQFF.
claims.source: Interestingly, B*35/FVS-isolated T cells from all donors displayed amino acid identical dominant complementary-determining region 3 (CDR3) of the α-chain, CAGNQGGKLIF (CDR3αCAGNQG), and β-chain, CASSLALDEQFF (CDR3βCASSLA; Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Both CDR3αCAGNQG and CDR3βCASSLA were identified in all samples sorted on B*35/IPS-tetramer binding and shown to be among the most dominant TCRs.
claims.source: Both CDR3αCAGNQG and CDR3βCASSLA were identified in all samples and shown to be among the most dominant TCRs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The public TCR was present in donor JZX which showed IPS/FVS-tetramer+ T cells below background level.
claims.source: Remarkably, this was also observed in donor JZX which showed IPS/FVS-tetramer+ T cells below background level, indicating that in more than 3 out of 37 donors, this public TCR is present. (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In more than 3 out of 37 donors, the public TCR is present.
claims.source: Remarkably, this was also observed in donor JZX which showed IPS/FVS-tetramer+ T cells below background level, indicating that in more than 3 out of 37 donors, this public TCR is present. (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of the public TCR in donor JZX.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells were able to recognize endogenously processed and presented peptide.
claims.source: Firstly, the reactivity of IPS/FVS-specific T cells against K562 transduced with the spike gene was measured which showed that the T cells were able to recognize endogenously processed and presented peptide (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific CD8+ T cells from a SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated donor were able to reduce intracellular SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies at both 0.05 and 0.5 MOI 24 hr post infection.
claims.source: SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific CD8+ T cells from a SARS-CoV-2 vaccinated donor were able to reduce intracellular SARS-CoV-2 RNA copies at both 0.05 and 0.5 multiplicity of infection (MOI) 24 hr post infection (Figure 6B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B–C.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells were able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 intracellular RNA copies in Calu-3 cells infected with 0.05 MOI.
claims.source: Interestingly, IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells were able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 intracellular RNA copies in Calu-3 cells infected with 0.05 MOI (MOI Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Incubating IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells with 0.5 MOI resulted in no difference in RNA copies compared to the no T cell control.
claims.source: Incubating with 10-fold more virus (0.5 MOI) resulted in no difference in RNA copies compared to the no T cell control (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-cross-reactive T cells were detected in two out of two CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ patients suffering from severe COVID-19.
claims.source: Interestingly, IPS/FVS-cross-reactive T cells were detected in two out of two CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ patients suffering from severe COVID-19, whereas the cross-reactive T cells were detected in 3 out of 37 healthy CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ donors (Figures 4C and 6E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR on IPS/FVS-specific T cells was lower compared to the SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells.
claims.source: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR was lower compared to the SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells and not considerably increased compared to IPS-specific T cells that were not cross-reactive with FVS (Figure 6D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claims.claim: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR on IPS/FVS-specific T cells was not considerably increased compared to IPS-specific T cells that were not cross-reactive with FVS.
claims.source: The expression of CD38 and HLA-DR was lower compared to the SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells and not considerably increased compared to IPS-specific T cells that were not cross-reactive with FVS (Figure 6D–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and are able to limit SARS-CoV-2 replication at low virus titers.
claims.source: These results indicate that IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells recognize SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and are able to limit SARS-CoV-2 replication at low virus titers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from the infection assays.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells did not show an activated phenotype during acute severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.source: However, IPS/FVS-specific T cells did not show an activated phenotype during acute severe SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.evidence: This is based on the flow cytometry data showing low expression of activation markers.

claims.claim: This is the first study to identify CMV-specific T cells that are cross reactive with SARS-CoV-2.
claims.source: To our knowledge this is the first study to identify CMV-specific T cells that are cross reactive with SARS-CoV-2.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claims.claim: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells recognized CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
claims.source: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells recognized CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM in HLA-DRB3*02:02 and were able to cross react with an as of yet unidentified, SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope in HLA-DRB3*02:02 (Weber et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays.

claims.claim: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells were able to cross react with an as of yet unidentified, SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
claims.source: The cross-reactive CD4+ T cells recognized CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM in HLA-DRB3*02:02 and were able to cross react with an as of yet unidentified, SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope in HLA-DRB3*02:02 (Weber et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays.

claims.claim: Previous studies have reported the presence of membrane-specific CD4+ T cell responses in SARS-CoV-2-unexposed donors utilizing the same commercially available membrane peptide pool.
claims.source: Previous studies have reported the presence of membrane-specific CD4+ T cell responses in SARS-CoV-2-unexposed donors utilizing the same commercially available membrane peptide pool, yet these studies did not aim to identify the peptide-HLA restriction (Bacher et al., 2020; Sekine et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bacher et al., 2020 and Sekine et al., 2020.

claims.claim: AGI-specific CD4+ T cells have been described to be cross reactive toward SARS-CoV-2 spike.
claims.source: AGI-specific CD4+ T cells have been described to be cross reactive toward SARS-CoV-2 spike which is in contrast to our finding (Weber et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weber et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells recognize the CMV epitope IPSINVHHY and SARS-CoV-2 epitope FVSNGTHWF presented in HLA-B*35:01.
claims.source: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells recognize the CMV epitope IPSINVHHY and SARS-CoV-2 epitope FVSNGTHWF presented in HLA-B*35:01.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from peptide identification assays.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific T cells were possibly detected previously but never further investigated or characterized.
claims.source: IPS/FVS-specific T cells were possibly detected previously but never further investigated or characterized (Shomuradova et al., 2020; Tarke et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shomuradova et al., 2020 and Tarke et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Both cross-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a higher avidity for the CMV epitope compared to the epitope derived from SARS-CoV-2.
claims.source: Both cross-reactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells displayed a higher avidity for the CMV epitope compared to the epitope derived from SARS-CoV-2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by peptide titration data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Other studies have reported an equal or even higher avidity for the SARS-CoV-2 epitope compared to the epitopes derived from the HCoV for which the T cells were hypothesized to be primed against.
claims.source: In contrast, other studies have reported an equal or even higher avidity for the SARS-CoV-2 epitope compared to the epitopes derived from the HCoV for which the T cells were hypothesized to be primed against (Braun et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021; Lineburg et al., 2021; Mateus et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Repeated exposure results in the selection of high avidity T cell clonotypes which are able to clear viral infection and protect against reinfection.
claims.source: This appears to be contradictive since it has been shown that repeated exposure results in the selection of high avidity T cell clonotypes which are able to clear viral infection and protect against reinfection (Abdel-Hakeem et al., 2017; Hombrink et al., 2013; Price et al., 2005; Schober et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Cross-reactive T cells would most likely display a higher avidity for the source pathogen compared to the avidity for SARS-CoV-2.
claims.source: Cross-reactive T cells would therefore most likely display a higher avidity for the source pathogen compared to the avidity for SARS-CoV-2, as reported in this study.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about T cell avidity and repeated exposure.

claims.claim: The contribution of other HCoVs as initial primers of the T cell response may have been over-estimated due to experimental design.
claims.source: Taken together, whereas cross-reactive T cells recognizing SARS-CoV-2 have been primarily described to be derived from other HCoVs, the contribution of these other HCoVs as initial primers of the T cell response may have been over-estimated due to experimental design.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the discussion of avidity and experimental design issues.

claims.claim: Further studies are required to identify other potential sources of cross reactivity with low sequence homology yet high prevalences such as CMV, EBV, influenza, or non-viral pathogens.
claims.source: Further studies are required to identify other potential sources of cross reactivity with low sequence homology yet high prevalences such as CMV, EBV, influenza, or non-viral pathogens.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claims.claim: Ex vivo detected heterologous CD8+ T cell immunity against two pathogens caused by dissimilar epitopes presented in the same HLA is rarely reported.
claims.source: Ex vivo detected heterologous CD8+ T cell immunity against two pathogens caused by dissimilar epitopes presented in the same HLA is rarely reported (Clute et al., 2005; Cornberg et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Clute et al., 2005 and Cornberg et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Heterologous immunity can be caused by the expression of a dual TCR.
claims.source: Heterologous immunity can be caused by the expression of a dual TCR which means that two TCR α- or β-chains are expressed simultaneously, resulting in two distinctive TCRs within one T cell (Cusick et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cusick et al., 2012.

claims.claim: A single TCR was identified in cross-reactive T cells, excluding the dual TCR hypothesis.
claims.source: However, here, we identified a single TCR in cross-reactive T cells excluding this hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TCR sequencing data.

claims.claim: Recognition of two distinct epitopes by a single TCR can be explained by shape similarity once the peptides are bound to the HLA molecule.
claims.source: Recognition of two distinct epitopes by a single TCR can be explained by shape similarity once the peptides are bound to the HLA molecule, and this shape similarity, or molecular mimicry can underpin T cell cross reactivity (Macdonald et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Macdonald et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Similarity between the IPS and FVS peptides in backbone conformation and the C-terminal part might underpin the T cell cross reactivity observed.
claims.source: Here, similarity between the IPS and FVS peptides in backbone conformation and the C-terminal part might underpin the T cell cross reactivity observed, as the majority of TCR docks preferentially toward the C-terminal of the peptide (Szeto et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling and supported by a citation to Szeto et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The majority of TCR docks preferentially toward the C-terminal of the peptide.
claims.source: Here, similarity between the IPS and FVS peptides in backbone conformation and the C-terminal part might underpin the T cell cross reactivity observed, as the majority of TCR docks preferentially toward the C-terminal of the peptide (Szeto et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Szeto et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The presence of cross-reactive memory T cells in circulation may be an advantage during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.source: The presence of these cross-reactive memory T cells in circulation may be an advantage during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection as rapid T cell responses were associated with less severe COVID-19 (Loyal et al., 2021; Sette and Crotty, 2021; Tan et al., 2021a).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Rapid T cell responses were associated with less severe COVID-19.
claims.source: The presence of these cross-reactive memory T cells in circulation may be an advantage during initial SARS-CoV-2 infection as rapid T cell responses were associated with less severe COVID-19 (Loyal et al., 2021; Sette and Crotty, 2021; Tan et al., 2021a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were less efficient compared to SARS-CoV-2-specific, vaccination-primed T cells in limiting viral spread in vitro.
claims.source: However, the cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were less efficient compared to SARS-CoV-2-specific, vaccination-primed T cells in limiting viral spread in vitro which can be explained by the reduced avidity of the cross-reactive T cells for the spike protein compared to CMV.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the infection assays shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells might be able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 spread at initial infection but likely do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19.
claims.source: These observations together indicate that IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells might be able to reduce SARS-CoV-2 spread at initial infection but likely do not play a significant role in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the activation state and functional data.

claims.claim: The study focused on circulating T cells, and it cannot be excluded that cross-reactive CD8+ T cells present in lung tissue displayed an activated phenotype.
claims.source: One limitation is that our study focused on circulating T cells, and we cannot exclude the possibility that cross-reactive CD8+ T cells present in lung tissue did display an activated phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claims.claim: Additional studies using larger cohorts are required to fully elucidate the potential role of cross-reactive CD8+ T cells in disease.
claims.source: In summary, additional studies using larger cohorts are required to fully elucidate the potential role of cross-reactive CD8+ T cells in disease.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claims.claim: Pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells can derive from non-homologous pathogens such as CMV.
claims.source: In conclusion, pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells can derive from non-homologous pathogens such as CMV.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: This expands the potential origin of pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell beyond other HCoVs.
claims.source: This expands the potential origin of these pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell beyond other HCoVs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were reactive toward dissimilar epitopes, and this cross reactivity was caused by a public TCR.
claims.source: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were reactive toward dissimilar epitopes, and this cross reactivity was caused by a public TCR, which has been rarely observed so far.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Cross-reactivity caused by a public TCR toward dissimilar epitopes has been rarely observed.
claims.source: The cross-reactive CD8+ T cells were reactive toward dissimilar epitopes, and this cross reactivity was caused by a public TCR, which has been rarely observed so far.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the rarity of this phenomenon in the literature.

claims.claim: The data points toward a role of the cross-reactive T cells in reducing SARS-CoV-2 viral load in the early stages of infection, prior to priming of SARS-CoV-2 specific T cells.
claims.source: Our data points toward a role of the cross-reactive T cells in reducing SARS-CoV-2 viral load in the early stages of infection, prior to priming of SARS-CoV-2 specific T cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the functional data from the infection assays.

claims.claim: These results aid in further understanding heterologous T cell immunity beyond common cold coronaviruses.
claims.source: Altogether, these results aid in further understanding heterologous T cell immunity beyond common cold coronaviruses and facilitate the investigation into the potential role of cross-reactive T cells in COVID-19.

claims.source: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells were characterized as CD154+CD137+, and memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells were identified based on expression of CD137 and IFN-γ (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological description supported by flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells were identified based on expression of CD137 and IFN-γ.
claims.source: Memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells were characterized as CD154+CD137+, and memory SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells were identified based on expression of CD137 and IFN-γ (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological description supported by flow cytometry data.

claims.claim: The FVS peptide might adopt a similar backbone conformation compared to the IPS peptide.
claims.source: Overall, the FVS peptide might adopt a similar backbone conformation compared to the IPS peptide, which would place in both peptides a small hydrophobic residue at position 6 (P6-T/V), a histidine at position 7, and a residue with a large side-chain at position 8 (P8-W/H).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling analysis.

claims.claim: The primary anchor in the FVS peptide is P2-V and P9-F.
claims.source: The primary anchor in the FVS peptide is P2-V and P9-F, both within the favored residues at those positions for HLA-B35-restricted peptide (Escobar et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling and supported by a citation to Escobar et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The lack of secondary anchor residue at position 5 in the FVS peptide (P5-N/G) might change the conformation of the central part of the peptide.
claims.source: The lack of secondary anchor residue at position 5 in the FVS peptide (P5-N/G) might change the conformation of the central part of the peptide that could be similar to the one observed in the spike-derived peptide IPF (S896-904) in complex with HLA-B*35:01 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Nguyen et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural modeling and supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Residue substitutions from the IPS to FVS peptide were possible without major steric clashes with the HLA or peptide residues.
claims.source: Residue substitutions from the IPS to FVS peptide were possible without major steric clashes with the HLA or peptide residues.

claims.claim: CD38 and HLA-DR are highly expressed on SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells during severe COVID-19.
claims.source: The activation state was measured by expression of activation markers CD38 and HLA-DR as these markers are highly expressed on SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells during severe COVID-19 (Figure 6D; Sekine et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sekine et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The prevalence of IPS/FVS-specific T cells in severe COVID-19 patients (2 out of 2) was higher than in healthy donors (3 out of 37).
claims.source: Interestingly, IPS/FVS-cross-reactive T cells were detected in two out of two CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ patients suffering from severe COVID-19, whereas the cross-reactive T cells were detected in 3 out of 37 healthy CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ donors (Figures 4C and 6E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the prevalence data between patient and donor cohorts.

results.result: SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses in pre-pandemic samples correlate with CMV seropositivity. CMV+ donors showed higher frequencies of SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells, particularly CD4+ responses to membrane peptides and CD8+ responses to spike peptides, which were accompanied by strong pp65 reactivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C27-C31 provide converging experimental evidence from flow cytometry showing that CMV+ donors (N=28) had detectable SARS-CoV-2-specific T cell responses not observed in CMV− donors (N=39), with statistical support from Figure 1. The correlation between membrane/spike responses and pp65 reactivity (C29, C31) strengthens the association.

results.result: Pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific CD4+ T cells originate from cross-reactive CMV-specific T cells. Clonally expanded CD4+ T cell clones recognized both SARS-CoV-2 membrane and CMV pp65 peptides, with higher avidity for CMV pp65 epitope AGILARNLVPM presented in HLA-DRB3*02:02.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C32-C37, C69-C70 provide experimental evidence from T cell cloning, peptide library screening, and HLA restriction assays (Figure 2). The demonstration that 20/27 clones responded to membrane peptides, and that specific clones recognized both antigens with higher avidity for CMV (C35) supports cross-reactivity. However, the SARS-CoV-2 membrane epitope remains unidentified (C70), which is a limitation.

results.result: Pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific CD8+ T cells originate from cross-reactive CMV-specific T cells. CD8+ T cell clones recognized both SARS-CoV-2 spike peptide FVSNGTHWF and CMV pp65 peptide IPSINVHHY, both presented by HLA-B*35:01, with higher avidity for the CMV peptide.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C38-C43, C73 provide strong experimental evidence from T cell cloning (23/28 clones reactive, all expressing same TCR), peptide identification via CPL assay, HLA restriction experiments, and peptide titration showing higher avidity for IPS (Figure 2). The convergence of multiple experimental approaches supports this cross-reactivity.

results.result: IPS/FVS cross-reactive CD8+ T cells are mediated by a public TCR found in multiple donors. Tetramer staining identified IPS/FVS-specific T cells in 3/37 healthy donors and 2/2 severe COVID-19 patients, all expressing identical CDR3α (CAGNQGGKLIF) and CDR3β (CASSLALDEQFF) sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C47-C51, C54-C58 provide strong evidence from tetramer staining (Figure 4) and TCR sequencing (Figure 5). The demonstration that all FVS-binding T cells also bind IPS (C48), the identical TCR sequences across donors (C54-C55), and detection in both healthy donors and COVID-19 patients (C7-C8, C51, C63) support the public TCR conclusion. The finding in donor JZX (C57-C58) extends the prevalence estimate.

results.result: Structural modeling suggests that IPS/FVS cross-reactivity is mediated by similarity in peptide backbone conformation and C-terminal residues. The peptides share limited sequence homology but have similar residues at key positions (P3-S, P6-T/V, P7-H, P9-F/Y) that may enable TCR recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C46, C85, C101-C104 present structural modeling based on the solved IPS-HLA-B*35:01 structure (Figure 3). The analysis identifies shared and similar residues and proposes a mechanism for cross-reactivity. However, this is computational modeling without experimental validation (e.g., crystal structure of TCR-pMHC complex), which limits certainty. The modeling is consistent with the functional data but requires experimental confirmation.

results.result: IPS/FVS-specific T cells display an effector memory phenotype with less differentiation compared to IPS-only specific T cells. Flow cytometry showed CCR7−CD45RA− phenotype in IPS/FVS-specific T cells from three donors.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4D showing phenotypic characterization of tetramer-positive cells. The effector memory phenotype is clearly demonstrated, and the comparison with IPS-specific T cells shows reduced differentiation. Sample size is limited (N=3 donors) but the data are consistent.

results.result: IPS/FVS-specific CD8+ T cells can recognize SARS-CoV-2-infected cells and reduce viral replication at low viral titers. In vitro infection assays showed that IPS/FVS-specific T cells reduced intracellular SARS-CoV-2 RNA at 0.05 MOI but not at 0.5 MOI, and were less efficient than vaccination-primed T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62, C66, C89 are supported by experimental data from K562 transduction experiments (C59, Figure 6A) and Calu-3 infection assays (C60-C62, Figure 6B-C). The dose-dependent effect (effective at low MOI but not high MOI) is clearly demonstrated with statistical significance. The comparison with vaccination-primed T cells (C89) provides important context about relative efficacy.

results.result: IPS/FVS-specific T cells are present in severe COVID-19 patients but do not show an activated phenotype during acute infection. These cells were detected in 2/2 CMV+ HLA-B*35:01+ severe COVID-19 patients but showed lower CD38/HLA-DR expression compared to SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65, C67, C90, C106 are supported by tetramer staining and activation marker analysis in COVID-19 patients (Figure 6D-E). The detection in 2/2 patients versus 3/37 healthy donors (C106) suggests enrichment, but the small patient cohort (N=2) limits statistical power. The lack of activation (C64-C65, C67) is clearly demonstrated but interpretation is complicated by the limitation to circulating T cells (C91).

results.result: CMV-specific T cells can cross-react with SARS-CoV-2 despite low sequence homology and may contribute to pre-existing immunity. This expands the potential origin of pre-pandemic SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells beyond other human coronaviruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C93-C95 are well-supported by the collective experimental evidence demonstrating cross-reactivity between dissimilar CMV and SARS-CoV-2 peptides. However, C12 and C97 regarding contribution to pre-existing immunity are speculative inferences based on the presence of these cells and their in vitro function, without direct evidence of protective effects in vivo. The conclusion is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: Cross-reactive T cells display higher avidity for CMV epitopes compared to SARS-CoV-2 epitopes, consistent with repeated CMV exposure. This pattern differs from some prior studies of HCoV cross-reactivity and suggests potential overestimation of HCoV contribution to pre-existing immunity.
results.evaluation: Claim C75 is directly supported by peptide titration data (Figure 2B, 2F). Claims C76-C78 provide context from literature and immunological principles. Claim C79 is a speculative inference about prior work, but is logically supported by the avidity data and discussion of experimental design issues in prior studies. The reasoning is sound but the conclusion about overestimation requires validation.

results.result: Background and context from prior literature on SARS-CoV-2 T cell immunity, pre-existing T cells, and heterologous immunity. These claims establish the scientific rationale for investigating CMV as a source of cross-reactive T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C26 are background claims supported by citations to published literature. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Discussion of novelty and mechanistic context. The study is the first to identify CMV-SARS-CoV-2 cross-reactive T cells, and cross-reactivity via a public TCR toward dissimilar epitopes is rarely observed. Dual TCR expression is excluded as a mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C81, C96 regarding novelty and rarity are supported by literature context (C71-C72, C74, C81). Claim C83 excluding dual TCR is supported by TCR sequencing showing single TCR. Claims C82, C84, C86 provide mechanistic context from literature. These are appropriate contextual claims that frame the significance of the findings.

results.result: Limitations and future directions. The study acknowledges limitations including focus on circulating T cells, small COVID-19 cohort, and need for larger studies. Speculative discussion of potential protective role of cross-reactive T cells in early infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C91-C92 appropriately acknowledge study limitations and call for future work. Claims C87-C88 are speculative about potential protective effects, supported by citations but not directly tested. These are appropriate caveats and future directions but do not constitute supported results.

results.result: Methodological approach for identifying SARS-CoV-2-specific T cells. CD4+ T cells were characterized as CD154+CD137+ and CD8+ T cells as CD137+IFN-γ+.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 describe the methodological approach supported by flow cytometry gating strategies (Figure 1A-B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This is standard methodology appropriately applied.

results.result: The TCRβ chain identified in IPS/FVS-specific T cells was previously described as IPS-specific in HLA-B*35:01.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by citation to Klarenbeek et al., 2012, providing independent validation of the TCR identification. This strengthens confidence in the peptide identification and TCR characterization.

results.result: CD38 and HLA-DR are established markers of T cell activation during severe COVID-19.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is a methodological justification supported by citation to Sekine et al., 2020. This is appropriate use of established markers for the phenotypic analysis.
